sec: Chronic hepatitis · etiologies, progression and laboratory monitoring

items.q: What are the most common (m/c) and second most common causes of chronic hepatitis in adults?
opts: NASH is most common, followed by alcohol as second most common
Hepatitis B is most common, followed by Hepatitis C
Alcohol is most common, followed by Wilson's disease
Autoimmune hepatitis is most common, followed by Budd-Chiari syndrome
items.exp: Under causes of chronic hepatitis, NASH is tagged '(m/c)' and alcohol as '(2nd m/c)'. (Book p997)

items.q: Match each clinical age group with its characteristic etiologies of chronic hepatitis — 1) Pediatric age group causes 2) Adult secondary causes … A) Autoimmune disease, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and biliary cirrhosis B) Cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis
items.exp: In children, causes are cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis; adult causes include autoimmune, Wilson's, hemochromatosis, Budd-Chiari, and biliary cirrhosis. (Book p997)

items.q: What is the expected life expectancy of a patient who enters decompensated cirrhosis without liver transplantation?
items.exp: Under decompensation in the disease progression chart, the text notes: '(Life expectancy 2 years without transplant)'. (Book p997)

items.q: Fill up: As chronic hepatitis progresses toward established cirrhosis, physical examination and imaging typically reveal gross ______ of the liver.
items.exp: Under cirrhosis in the progression flowchart, the text notes 'Shrinkage of liver seen'. (Book p997)

items.q: What is the most common (m/c) constitutional symptom signalling disease progression in chronic hepatitis?
items.exp: Under progression features, fatigue is explicitly annotated with '(m/c)'. (Book p997)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a clinical symptom indicating progression of chronic hepatitis?
items.exp: Features of progression listed are Fatigue (m/c), Altered sleep rhythm, Muscle wasting, Loss of libido, and Hepatomegaly; fever is not among them. (Book p997)

items.q: During routine clinical examination of a patient with suspected progressive chronic hepatitis, hepatomegaly is palpated. What is the indicated quantitative test to ascertain the degree of fibrosis?
items.exp: The flowchart notes that if hepatomegaly is seen: 'Fibroscan : Quantitative test to ascertain degree of fibrosis'. (Book p997)

items.q: What laboratory transaminase pattern and numerical ceiling are typical of uncomplicated chronic hepatitis?
opts: ALT/AST elevation < 150 U/L with ALT > AST
ALT/AST elevation > 1000 U/L with AST > ALT
items.exp: Under laboratory investigation for chronic hepatitis, the line reads: 'ALT/AST ↑ (<150 U/L) with ALT > AST'. (Book p997)

items.q: Assess the two statements on chronic hepatitis: I Patients with chronic hepatitis are usually asymptomatic and frequently detected on routine screening with LFTs. II Once cirrhosis develops, the three major life-threatening pathways are portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver failure.
items.exp: Both statements are true: chronic hepatitis is usually asymptomatic and found on LFT screening, and cirrhosis leads to portal HTN, HCC, and liver failure. (Book p997)

items.q: A 44-year-old man with obesity and dyslipidemia undergoes a health checkup. He feels mildly fatigued but has no jaundice or ascites. LFTs show ALT 82 U/L and AST 54 U/L (both <150 U/L, ALT > AST). What is the primary management strategy for his liver enzyme monitoring?
opts: Continuous monitoring of liver enzymes along with evaluation for NASH
Immediate emergency referral for orthotopic liver transplantation
Initiation of intravenous high-dose N-acetylcysteine therapy
items.exp: The management section highlights 'Continuous monitoring of liver enzymes' and screening for treatable causes such as NASH. (Book p997)

items.q: Fill up: In children, chronic hepatitis progressing to early cirrhosis may be caused by ______ deficiency or Indian childhood cirrhosis.
items.exp: Pediatric causes listed include cholestasis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and Indian childhood cirrhosis. (Book p997)
